name: Mahila Atma Raksha Samiti (MARS)
summaryCard: Bengal women's self-defence organisation whose members took an active, sometimes armed, role in Tebhaga sharecropper mobilisation alongside the Kisan Sabha.
fullEntry: MARS grew out of anti-famine and anti-fascist women's organising in Bengal in the early 1940s and became closely linked with Communist Party and Kisan Sabha networks. During the Tebhaga movement, MARS cadres organised women bargadar households, took part in crop-guarding actions, and in some accounts participated directly in resisting police and landlord agents alongside male Kisan Sabha members.

sources.citation: Multiple secondary accounts of the Tebhaga movement note organised women's participation, sometimes attributed to MARS

editorNote: General claim of women's organised participation is well corroborated across sources; MARS's specific institutional role in Tebhaga (as opposed to women's participation more broadly) should be checked against a dedicated MARS history before publishing.

name: Sunil Sen
role: Historian and Kisan Sabha participant; author of the primary scholarly account of the movement
summaryCard: Communist activist and later historian whose 1972 monograph 'Agrarian Struggle in Bengal, 1946-47' remains the standard scholarly account of Tebhaga.
fullEntry: Sen was involved in the Kisan Sabha's peasant organising in Bengal and later wrote what is widely regarded as the foundational historical study of the Tebhaga movement, drawing on his own participation as well as archival and field research.

sources.citation: Sunil Sen, Agrarian Struggle in Bengal, 1946-47, People's Publishing House, 1972

name: Kampram Singh
role: Kisan Sabha organizer, North Bengal (Dinajpur area)
summaryCard: Cited across several sources as a key organiser of Tebhaga in North Bengal, particularly among Rajbanshi and Santhal sharecroppers.
fullEntry: Named alongside Bhawan Singh in multiple secondary accounts as a leading local organiser during the movement's earliest and most intense phase in Dinajpur district.

sources.citation: Testbook and Vajiram & Ravi UPSC study notes both name Kampram/Kompram Singh as a movement leader

editorNote: Spelling varies across sources (Kampram/Kompram Singh Sanyal). Role and exact contribution should be checked against Sunil Sen's monograph.

title: Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha conference at Panjia
summaryCard: The Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha's conference at Panjia first raised the tebhaga demand — six years before the mass movement of 1946-47.
fullEntry: At its June 1940 conference in Panjia, Jessore district, the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha called for sharecroppers to receive two-thirds of the harvest rather than half. Wartime conditions and the 1943 Bengal famine delayed any large-scale action on this demand until 1946.

sources.citation: The Tebhaga Movement: A Revolutionary Peasant Uprising in Bengal, PolSci Institute

title: Tebhaga spreads through North Bengal
summaryCard: Following the initial Dinajpur outbreak, the movement spread through Rangpur, Jalpaiguri, and Malda, with Santhal and Rajbanshi sharecroppers leading direct land-occupation actions.
fullEntry: Adivasi communities, particularly Santhals and Rajbanshis, played a leading role in North Bengal's Tebhaga actions, in some accounts occupying over 1,000 acres of land by early 1947 as part of enforcing the crop-division demand directly in the fields.

sources.citation: Tebhaga movement, Grokipedia

editorNote: The '1,000+ acres occupied' figure originates from an AI-generated encyclopedia entry (Grokipedia), not a primary or academic secondary source. Treat as unverified until corroborated elsewhere.

title: Uprising in South 24 Parganas
summaryCard: Tebhaga-related peasant uprising broke out across several South 24 Parganas localities, including Kakdwip, Bhangar, Sonarpur, and Canning.
fullEntry: South 24 Parganas became one of the movement's active fronts outside North Bengal, with sharecroppers in several localities asserting the tebhaga demand and clashing with landlords' agents and police.

sources.citation: Tebhaga Movement (1946-1947), IAS Site

title: Movement spreads to Mymensingh, Jessore, and Khulna
summaryCard: Alongside North Bengal and 24 Parganas, the East Bengal districts of Mymensingh, Jessore, and Khulna became severe and violent centres of the movement.
fullEntry: By late 1946, the Tebhaga movement had spread across roughly 19 of undivided Bengal's 27 districts, with Mymensingh and the Jessore-Khulna belt named among the areas of most intense activity in eastern Bengal.

sources.citation: A Struggle for Fair Share: Recounting the Tebhaga Movement, 1946-47, Labour File

title: Clashes at Kakdwip
summaryCard: Kakdwip, in South 24 Parganas, was the site of significant peasant-police confrontation during the Tebhaga movement.
fullEntry: Details of the specific incident(s) at Kakdwip need further research — it is consistently named as a flashpoint but a precise account of events, casualties, and dates has not yet been assembled here.

sources.citation: Tebhaga Movement (1946-1947), IAS Site

editorNote: This entry is a placeholder flagging Kakdwip's significance — needs a specific, dated account of what actually happened there, ideally from Sunil Sen's monograph or a district-level study.

title: Organised participation of women in Tebhaga
summaryCard: Women, including through the Mahila Atma Raksha Samiti, took an active and in some accounts armed role in Tebhaga actions — guarding crops, attending meetings, and confronting police and landlords' agents.
fullEntry: Multiple accounts of the Tebhaga movement note the significant and organised role women played, a notable departure from more limited female participation in many earlier peasant and nationalist movements in the region.

sources.citation: Tebhaga Movement, Causes, Features, Impacts, UPSC Notes, Vajiram & Ravi

title: Communal violence and Partition weaken the movement
summaryCard: The communal violence surrounding Partition in 1946-47 divided Bengal's peasantry along religious lines, fracturing the unified front the Kisan Sabha had built and contributing to the movement's decline.
fullEntry: As Bengal moved toward Partition, communal polarisation diverted political energy and split the peasant coalition the Tebhaga movement depended on, compounding the effect of state repression.

sources.citation: The Tebhaga Movement: A Revolutionary Peasant Uprising in Bengal, PolSci Institute

title: Bargadari Act passed
summaryCard: Years after the movement's peak, the Bargadari Act formally recognised sharecroppers' entitlement to two-thirds of the produce where they supplied the inputs — the movement's core demand, partially codified into law.
fullEntry: The Bargadari Act of 1950 represented a delayed, partial legislative outcome of the tebhaga demand, distinct from and later than the 1947 Bengal Bargadars Temporary Regulation Bill.

sources.citation: Tebhaga Movement, ClearIAS
